newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian giant grapples with copper price.
newsitem.headline: Australian giant grapples with copper price.

text.p: Australia's largest company, Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd (BHP), said on Tuesday that it was struggling with its copper and steel operations.
The news from BHP, the world's second largest copper producer and a leading regional steel-maker, dragged its share price lower on a day when the overall sharemarket was stronger.

BHP shares ended 24 cents down at A$16.60, with brokers saying the comments by managing director John Prescott inflamed the already negative sentiment surrounding the stock after two brokers issued critical reports.
"I think that at the moment, the real challenge for BHP is the copper price and the company's performance in the copper sector," Prescott said in an interview with Reuters.
BHP's exposure to the copper market increased in January when it paid $2.4 billion for Magma Copper Co, and combined the US-based company with operations in Papua New Guinea and Chile.

But since the Magma purchase, copper prices have fallen by about 25 US cents a pound to about 90 cents, weakened by growing supplies, lower demand and the mid-year trading scandal involving Sumitomo Corp. Each one US cent rise adds A$16 million to BHP's bottom line, Prescott said.
BHP has hedged itself from further falls in copper prices and would have to rely on better prices for products in its other divisions until the global market improved, he said.

"Steel prices are not too good and copper prices are poor, but on the other hand, our iron ore and coal prices are slightly better than they were last year and oil prices are a lot better than we expected they would be," he said.

Prescott said the sharp rise in the Australian dollar this year to 80 US cents from 73 US cents in January was also affecting overall profitability, with a one-cent gain reducing profits by A$40 million.
BHP, the only steel producer in Australia, believed global conditions had deteriorated, especially with reduced demand in key Asian markets, where local competition was growing.
Asked if the global steel market was getting better, Prescott said after delivering a speech in Sydney: "No, is the short answer."
BHP, the largest company in Australia by market capitalisation, had a 14 percent fall in 1995/96 (June-May) net profit to A$1.05 billion (US$840 million), with the steel division falling 76 percent.
Trading in the first quarter has shown some improvement in margins for steel, "but not by much," Prescott said.
"It is a long, tough slog," he said.

Prescott said the world steel industry suffered from "inventory issues," compounded by new production and structural changes in Japan where many manufacturing operations had moved offshore to cheaper locations.
